title: Uncertainty Is Not Communicated Usefully
summary: This page defines an AI-specific interpretation failure: uncertainty exists in a model's output but is not communicated in a form that supports calibrated human judgment. The documented Puraite example shows how Creative Navy handled confidence and reasoning in AI-assisted systematic literature review interfaces.
keyFacts: The failure concerns AI-specific uncertainty: the reliability variation of AI system outputs and the interface's failure to communicate that variation usefully.
The problem is not that uncertainty exists, but that model uncertainty is not surfaced in a form the user can act on.
A confidence signal must be visible at the decision point, not hidden behind an additional interaction.
Useful uncertainty communication requires a graded signal, not only a binary reliable/unreliable flag.
A confidence score is not fully actionable without enough reasoning or evidence for the user to evaluate it.
In the Puraite case, Creative Navy designed AI screening and data extraction review interfaces for AI-assisted systematic literature review.
The Puraite suggestion display required four iteration cycles before the direct quote from the publication was placed visibly in the side panel from the outset of the decision interaction.
Puraite's data extraction flow communicated AI confidence as explicit percentages with colour-coded scanning support.
No dedicated user research was possible in the Puraite engagement; a Creative Navy team member's firsthand systematic review software experience served as the domain learning proxy.
The Puraite outcome evidence is client-reported and indirect; no task-time, error-rate, or baseline research data was collected.

bodySections.heading: Definition: AI Uncertainty Is Not Communicated Usefully
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Uncertainty is not communicated usefully when an AI system produces outputs with varying confidence but the interface presents those outputs as uniformly reliable results. The user sees an AI output that looks complete and plausible, but does not receive the confidence information and reasoning needed to decide whether to accept it, verify it, or override it.

The failure is not the existence of uncertainty. AI systems that perform non-trivial reasoning produce outputs with different levels of certainty, different evidence bases, and different structural reliability. The failure occurs when that variation remains inside the system and is not surfaced in a form that supports calibrated human judgment.

bodySections.heading: Failure Pattern: AI Outputs Appear More Uniform Than Their Reliability
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
An AI product that displays every output with the same apparent reliability creates two predictable user responses. Users may over-trust outputs that the AI itself has low confidence in, or they may treat every output with uniform scepticism and verify everything. Both responses are miscalibrated relative to the system's actual reliability profile.

The interface-level mechanism is simple: the AI output is displayed as a result rather than as an estimate. It appears present and plausible, but lacks the information that would allow the user to judge the AI's confidence in what it produced.

This failure is a specific AI-context instance of a broader interpretation problem: users can see information but cannot judge what matters. In the AI uncertainty case, the missing judgment concerns which AI outputs warrant verification.

bodySections.heading: Useful AI Uncertainty Communication Must Be Visible at the Decision Point
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A confidence signal is only operationally useful when it is visible at the moment the user must accept, verify, or override an AI output. If confidence information exists only in a detail view, explanation panel, or separate confidence summary screen, the interface imposes an additional cost before the user can decide whether verification is warranted.

That additional interaction cost compounds across review sessions with many decisions. When accessing confidence information costs more time than the benefit of having it, users stop accessing it. The oversight mechanism remains nominally available but becomes operationally unused.

This is a design failure, not a lazy-user problem. The interface has made oversight more costly than it can be under real use conditions. Confidence information that requires an additional interaction will be used for edge cases and skipped for decisions that feel routine, even though AI confidence variation does not necessarily track the user's sense of routine work.

bodySections.heading: Useful AI Uncertainty Communication Must Be Graded Rather Than Binary
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A binary uncertainty flag does not communicate the variation an AI system actually produces. AI systems do not normally generate only two meaningful reliability classes, such as reliable and unreliable. They produce a distribution of confidence across outputs.

For review work, a 95%-confidence extraction and a 52%-confidence extraction require different responses. The first may support quick review; the second may warrant the scrutiny appropriate to an unreliable draft. Treating both as the same class prevents efficient allocation of verification effort.

A useful interface presents confidence as a graded signal that users can scan. The purpose is not to make users inspect every output equally. The purpose is to let users maintain review pace while directing attention to lower-confidence outputs where oversight is more likely to matter.

bodySections.heading: Useful AI Uncertainty Communication Must Include Enough Reasoning to Evaluate the Score
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A confidence score alone is not always actionable. A model that is 70% confident because it misread a publication is different from a model that is 70% confident because the evidence is genuinely ambiguous. The numeric confidence may be the same, but the epistemic basis is different.

Users who need to exercise judgment require enough reasoning to evaluate the AI's confidence. In practice, this means showing the evidence the model used to reach its conclusion, not only the confidence level assigned to the conclusion.

The design tension is that full reasoning can slow the interface down, while too little reasoning prevents meaningful oversight. A useful interface resolves this structurally: confidence and reasoning are visible without additional interaction, arranged so users can scan quickly or evaluate deeply from the same decision context.

bodySections.heading: Puraite: AI Uncertainty Communication in Systematic Literature Review
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Puraite is a web application for AI-assisted systematic literature reviews. The review process involves screening large volumes of publications against inclusion and exclusion criteria, then extracting structured data from qualifying studies. Puraite integrates AI assistance into initial screening decisions, criteria suggestions, and data extraction.

In the Puraite case, reviewers encountered AI outputs at decision points and had to decide whether to accept or override them. The documented design challenge focused on the AI screening screen and the data extraction flow, both of which required uncertainty communication that supported review pace and calibrated judgment.

The Puraite engagement ran for 7 months as an Implementation Partnership. No dedicated user research was possible within the engagement timeline, so a Creative Navy team member's direct firsthand experience using systematic review software served as the domain learning proxy.

bodySections.heading: Puraite Screening Design: Direct Evidence Visible Without an Extra Step
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed the Puraite screening interface by treating good AI behaviour as a design problem, not only as a model problem. The screening interaction required reviewers to assess AI inclusion and exclusion decisions quickly across many publications while retaining the ability to make substantive overrides.

Two failure modes were identified from first principles. A display that was too compact would make reviewers accept AI outputs because examining them closely cost too much time. A display that was too detailed would slow reviewers enough that AI assistance no longer produced useful efficiency.

Creative Navy-recorded engagement evidence states that four iteration cycles on the suggestion display were required before the resolution was found. Versions that provided full criteria and evidence required expansion or navigation, which broke the screening rhythm. Versions that compressed the display for scan speed removed the evidence needed for substantive override decisions.

The resolved design placed the direct quote from the publication in the side panel from the start of the decision interaction. The reviewer could see the AI decision, the criteria applied, and the specific text evidence simultaneously. Confidence information and reasoning were present at the decision point without an additional interaction.

bodySections.heading: Puraite Data Extraction Design: Confidence Percentages Supported Scanning
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Puraite data extraction component required a different uncertainty communication decision. Project managers and reviewers needed to scan a table of AI-extracted values and identify which extractions warranted attention.

The documented design communicated AI confidence as an explicit percentage with colour-coded scanning support. Lower-confidence extractions were visually marked for attention, so reviewers did not have to examine every extraction individually before allocating verification effort.

The design treated a 52%-confidence extraction and a 95%-confidence extraction differently. The interface supported verification where it was most needed instead of forcing either uniform scrutiny or uninformed trust.

bodySections.heading: Puraite Product Finding: Blinded Screening Was Identified but Not Designed
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Puraite engagement also raised a product-level question: when should AI decisions be withheld from reviewers entirely to prevent the AI recommendation from biasing independent judgment? This was identified as a blinded screening mode with interface implications.

The detailed design of blinded screening was not in scope for the engagement. Its identification remains a finding from the work, not a completed design resolution.

bodySections.heading: eToro as a Bounded Non-AI Analogue for Decision-Point Uncertainty
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
eToro is a bounded analogue for this failure, not a co-equal AI example. The uncertainty in eToro was market and outcome uncertainty at a financial decision point, not AI confidence.

The pre-redesign buy flow presented a trade as a price-and-quantity confirmation. That framing communicated an implied single expected result and did not give the user a usable sense of the range of outcomes a position could produce.

The redesigned flow introduced structured scenario framing. It presented how a position might behave under different market movements as uncertainty ranges rather than predictions, with downside exposure visible at the moment of commitment rather than discoverable afterwards.

The documented behavioural confirmation was a randomised A/B result: conversion changed from 5.1% to 7.4%, time-to-trade changed from 11.8 minutes to 8.6 minutes, with no increase in drop-off and no reduction in exploration depth. This evidence measures decision efficiency and coherence, not uncertainty-communication quality directly. The relevance is the removed mechanism: single-value framing was replaced with structured-range framing at the decision point.

The regulatory framing in the eToro example is also bounded. The uncertainty ranges were not AI predictions, and the reference to MiFID II / SEC-FINRA rules concerns risk communication that must not imply a guaranteed outcome.

bodySections.heading: How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Addresses AI Uncertainty Communication
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method designs software whose interfaces, workflows, and operating logic carry real operational consequences, working through five phases — Sandbox Experiments, Concept Convergence, Iterative System Building, Organizational Integration, and Implementation Partnership — to take each system from initial exploration to independent operation by the client's own team.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses this failure by defining good AI behaviour as a design problem. In this context, good behaviour means presenting AI uncertainty at decision points in a form that supports both calibrated human judgment and the pace of real work.

There is no generic interface solution for this problem. The right uncertainty display depends on the task, the user, the volume and pace of decisions, and the form of reasoning the AI produces in the domain. In systematic review, the evidence unit was the publication text passage used by the AI. In other domains, the relevant evidence unit may differ.

The transferable principle is that reasoning should be visible at the decision point without additional interaction. The specific implementation is not transferable without design work. In the Puraite case, the direct-quote-in-side-panel resolution emerged through iteration because compressed designs failed the override-quality requirement and expanded designs failed the scan-speed requirement.

bodySections.heading: Boundary: AI Confidence Uncertainty Is Not Source-Provenance Uncertainty
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
This page concerns AI-specific uncertainty: a model's knowledge of its own output. It does not cover uncertainty inherited from source provenance, such as where a value came from, when it was measured, or whether it still holds.

This page should also be distinguished from broader relevance and priority judgment failures. The broad failure is that users see information but cannot judge what matters. The AI-specific failure is that users cannot judge which AI outputs warrant verification because the interface does not communicate confidence and reasoning usefully.

Non-AI systems that label an outcome unknown may look similar at the interface level, but they do not represent AI confidence communication unless a model is estimating the reliability of its own output. Cases involving uncertainty from sources, links, protocols, clocks, or inherited data belong outside this page's scope.
